title: Frumentius in Ethiopia
hook: a boy spared when his ship is attacked helps raise a prince, and comes back a bishop

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bede, who died one sentence from the end of his translation. Your line was finish the work. What did you finish? Day seven hundred ninety-five.

Two boys are sitting under a tree with their books, studying, while the grown-ups go ashore for water. Remember that tree. For days we've been in the cold north, with monks, islands and harps. Today the map swings far to the south. A teacher from the city of Tyre is sailing home with two young relatives, Frumentius and his brother Aedesius. The ship puts in at a harbor. And the people there, the old account says, are at odds with the Romans. They attack, and everyone on the ship is killed, except two boys found under a tree, reading.
screen: `A SHIP PUTS IN AT A HARBOR.`

segments.voice: The story is told by Rufinus, a church historian who says he heard it from Aedesius himself, years later. The boys are taken to the king. The king likes them. Aedesius becomes his cupbearer. Frumentius, the sharper of the two, is put in charge of the royal records and accounts. Then the king dies. He leaves a young son, and before he dies he sets the two foreigners free. They could go home. But the queen asks them to stay and help run the kingdom until the prince is grown, and they do. Frumentius uses his position quietly. He looks for Christian merchants passing through from the Roman world, and helps them set up places to meet and pray. When the prince comes of age, the brothers hand everything back and leave. Aedesius goes home to Tyre. Frumentius goes to Alexandria, to the bishop there, Athanasius, and says: there are Christians in that land, and they need a bishop. Athanasius listens, and answers, in effect: who could we find better than you? He makes Frumentius a bishop and sends him straight back. The old writers call the place India, a word they used loosely. Historians connect it with the kingdom of Aksum, in what is now Ethiopia and Eritrea. Ethiopian Christians remember Frumentius as their own, and call him Abba Salama, father of peace. And now the carry. In the Ethiopian Orthodox church, the altar holds a tabot, a tablet that stands for the tablets of the covenant kept in the ark. Ethiopian tradition says the ark itself rests in Ethiopia. So a church of the ark, begun with two boys under a tree.

Here's the practice: learn one fact about Ethiopia. You've already learned a few today: Abba Salama, the tabot on the altar, the ark the tradition speaks of. Settle, and breathe. Choose the one that stays with you. Hold it the way you'd hold a small, unfamiliar object someone handed you, turning it over, noticing it. Then let your mind go to the people who carry that fact every day as their own, in Ethiopia and wherever Ethiopians live now. If you pray, you can pray for them. If you don't, just hold them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Frumentius. The boy who survived a massacre in Ethiopia, served a king, stayed to help a queen, and came back as a bishop. Abba Salama.
Your line: the church of the ark. Today, look up one more thing about Ethiopia's church, or its people, that you didn't know this morning. Day seven hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Christians honor Frumentius as Abba Salama, and their churches keep a tabot, a consecrated tablet, on the altar; at the feast of Timkat, the tabots are carried in procession.

fork.setup: you're Frumentius. the king who took you in has died and set you free. you could sail home. the queen asks you to stay and help until her son is grown. what do you do?

stay and help run the kingdom.

original.note: Ge'ez: tabot, the consecrated tablet on the altar of an Ethiopian Orthodox church.

trapdoor: what you thought: a missionary sent to Africa.
what it means: a boy spared when his ship was attacked, who served a king, stayed to help, and asked Alexandria to send a bishop, and was sent back as that bishop himself.
what a scholar hears: Rufinus, who says he had the story from Aedesius himself, and calls the place India, a word the ancients used loosely.

notes: The index hook said 'shipwrecked' and 'Ethiopia's first bishop (4th century)'. In Rufinus the ship is attacked in harbor, not wrecked; per the claims rule the hook field and script give no century and no 'first'. Confirm.

Rufinus 10.9–10 (also Socrates 1.19): Meropius of Tyre; the boys under a tree; Aedesius cupbearer, Frumentius over records/accounts; the dying king frees them; the queen's request; Christian merchants and places of prayer; Athanasius's answer; Rufinus's source in Aedesius. Paraphrased; confirm. The script doesn't name Meropius.
'The Red Sea coast of Africa' and 'the old writers call it India, a word they used loosely': identification with Aksum is scholarly, not in Rufinus. Confirm wording.
Abba Salama glossed as 'father of peace': confirm the gloss with an Ethiopian Orthodox Keeper; he is also called Kesate Birhan.

Tabot, and the tradition that the Ark of the Covenant rests in Ethiopia (at Aksum): attributed to Ethiopian tradition; confirm phrasing with a Keeper. Ge'ez spelling ታቦት: confirm. Timkat procession in howItsDone: confirm.
